{"id": "79:41/q09", "question": "How does the promise of Paradise fit the surrounding passage and surah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:41/q09/p1", "position": "It completes the contrast between the rebellious and the God-fearing after the proof of resurrection, directing listeners toward lasting reward.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the surah establishes resurrection and gathering and displays humanity's final fate, with its oaths marking a decisive climax after preceding surahs' exposition. Ibn ʿĀshūr says judgment and the warning and glad tidings follow proof of resurrection; the wise choose lasting reward over passing pleasure. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says Hell's people come first because polytheists are being addressed. Islahi contrasts the disobedient fate with glad tidings for those who feared God; Kuranyolu describes opposed attitudes ending in loss or salvation; Study Quran locates the believers/disbelievers contrast in verses 34–41."}]}
{"id": "79:41/q10", "question": "About whom were these verses reportedly revealed?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in named figures, including the brother's name, and in their accounts of Badr and Uḥud.", "positions": [{"id": "79:41/q10/p1", "position": "Musʿab ibn ʿUmayr and his brother Abū ʿAzīz are linked to the opposed outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports that Musʿab killed his brother at Uḥud and defended the Messenger until struck by arrows; al-Rāzī gives the same setting but says spears pierced him. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Ālūsī, calls one brother tyrannical and worldly and Musʿab fearful and restrained. Al-Ālūsī also reports Musʿab's protection of the Prophet and death by arrows, with the Prophet's words of entrusting him to God and recalling his two cloaks and golden sandal strap. His citation of al-Kashshāf calls the brother captured and says their mother was exceptionally wealthy. Al-Māwardī names only Musʿab in his revelation report; these accounts vary in details of capture, killing, and arrows or spears."}, {"id": "79:41/q10/p2", "position": "Musʿab and his brother ʿĀmir are the two figures.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās: ʿĀmir was captured at Badr, identified himself as Musʿab's brother, and initially received kind treatment before Musʿab told his captors to bind him."}, {"id": "79:41/q10/p3", "position": "Abū Jahl and Musʿab are linked to the two verses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as another account from Ibn ʿAbbās."}, {"id": "79:41/q10/p4", "position": "The first of the two verses concerns al-Naḍr and his son al-Ḥārith.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī records this additional report without assigning the Paradise verse separately."}]}
{"id": "79:41/q11", "question": "What is meant by reports of the Quran's seven letters and Paradise's seven gates?", "turns_on": "Whether 'seven letters' names variant Arabic wording or distinct meanings, and whether the seven gates tradition is about Quranic themes rather than conflicting recitations.", "positions": [{"id": "79:41/q11/p1", "position": "The seven letters in recitation are Arabic tongues; the seven gates point to Quranic contents that lead practitioners to Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites established reports through ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy and others in which the Prophet approved differing recitations and said God commanded seven letters. He argues that their dispute concerned wording, since they accepted the Quran's commands, prohibitions, promises, warnings, prophetic arguments, admonitions, and parables. Semantically opposed variants would make God command, forbid, and permit the same act, contradict Q 4:82, and imply the Prophet gave opposing judgments for one matter. Ibn Kathīr reports al-Ṭabarī's point that Arab dialects exceed seven, so the Quran came in some Arabic tongues; he also transmits reports from Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd that the Quran descended from seven gates of Paradise, and al-Ṭabarī's gloss of these as commands, prohibitions, encouragement, warning, stories, and parables."}, {"id": "79:41/q11/p2", "position": "The seven aspects are Quranic themes such as commands, prohibitions, exhortation, warnings, stories, and parables, distinct from the recitation reports.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says advocates of the thematic account do not claim it explains the earlier recitation reports; they mean the Quran came in seven aspects, as transmitted from the Prophet and Companions. He frames the question of evidence for the dialect account over the thematic one. Al-Ṭabarī himself explains the seven gates as Quranic meanings leading practitioners to Paradise."}, {"id": "79:41/q11/p3", "position": "The seven letters are seven divergent meanings, including conflicting legal or doctrinal meanings.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies this opposing interpretation and rejects it: conflicting meanings would affirm contradiction in the Quran despite Q 4:82, make one act simultaneously commanded, forbidden, and permitted, and attribute opposed judgments on one matter to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q01", "question": "What is the Hour's مُنتَهَىٰهَآ?", "turns_on": "Whether 'end' denotes the limit of knowledge, its lexical endpoint, the reach of its news, or the end of the created order; some explain a shift from spatial endpoint to knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q01/p1", "position": "Its end is the limit of knowledge of the Hour, held by God alone, especially knowledge of its appointed time.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi's Abu Ishaq and exegetes, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj gloss the end as the limit of knowledge or knowledge with God. Al-Nahhas says it is the endpoint of knowledge. Al-Kashshaf says no created being has received it; al-Alusi's first interpretation says no one shares any part of it. Al-Alusi's preceding interpretation, Elmalili, and Tabatabai extend the scope to the Hour's essence, reality, properties, and details, as well as its time; Asad calls it the beginning and end of all that can be known. Ibn Ashur explains that an omitted noun is 'knowledge of its time'; he cites 53:42. Al-Qurtubi cites 7:187 and 31:34; Ibn Kathir cites 7:187, and the Prophet's answer to Gabriel that the questioned knows no more than the questioner, also reported by Study Quran. Mawardi says God concealed five matters even from a near angel or sent prophet and cites the end of 31:34; Kuran Yolu also cites 31:34. Study Quran says God will manifest the Hour at its appointed time and cites 7:187 and 30:34. Tabatabai says its sudden arrival in 7:187 supports divine exclusivity, while observing that reconciliation with other verses needs reflection. Al-Qashani adds that knowing it requires annihilation of one's knowledge in divine knowledge and one's self in God. Al-Durr's Ibn Jurayj also reads the following evening and morning as worldly time."}, {"id": "79:44/q01/p2", "position": "Muntahā literally denotes the place or point where something reaches its end, later extending to destiny and knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi gives the terminal-place sense. Ibn Ashur traces its shift from a journey's endpoint to destiny and then knowledge."}, {"id": "79:44/q01/p3", "position": "Its end may be the point at which news of the Hour reaches someone.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports this as an alternative to the interpretation through knowledge of its time."}, {"id": "79:44/q01/p4", "position": "The Hour's end may be the extinction of things and causes, when God's sole dominion becomes manifest.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reports this alternative and says even time cannot truly delimit the Hour."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q02", "question": "How is مُنتَهَىٰهَآ construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q02/p1", "position": "It is a nominative subject, with 'knowledge of its time' understood in the expression.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas calls muntahāhā nominative as subject. Ibn Ashur supplies the omitted noun 'knowledge of its time,' referring back to the question in 79:42."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q03", "question": "How does this statement answer the preceding question about the Hour?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement directly explains the Prophet's inability to answer the timing question or follows a pause after a question already rejected by his mission as the last prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q03/p1", "position": "It redirects the question about the Hour's time to God, because the Prophet has not been given that knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya say the Prophet has no role in fixing its time; Ibn Ashur says the statement explains that lack of involvement. Al-Qurtubi's report from al-Zuhri through Urwa presents it as an answer to the Prophet's frequent questioning and an instruction not to seek the time. Kuran Yolu says God's question establishes that the Prophet cannot obtain this knowledge. Al-Alusi says, on one interpretation, the Prophet was only to announce its approach and, on another, the question to him is misplaced because all knowledge of it belongs to God. Nasafi's first interpretation confines knowledge of its timing to God."}, {"id": "79:44/q03/p2", "position": "The question is rejected because the last Prophet's mission itself signals the Hour; a pause after 'in what' leaves this verse as an independent statement.", "reasons": "Nasafi reports this alternative and the possible pause after the preceding phrase."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q04", "question": "What happened when people asked about the Hour, according to the reports?", "turns_on": "Whether the repeated questions were asked by the Prophet or addressed to him; Tabatabai objects to the first reading from the context.", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q04/p1", "position": "The Prophet himself questioned repeatedly, then ceased when the verse placed the Hour's knowledge with God.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi transmits al-Zuhri through Urwa that the Prophet's frequent questioning was answered by this verse and he was told not to seek the time. {"id": "79:44/q05", "question": "What task concerning the Hour is assigned to the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q05/p1", "position": "He is to warn those who fear the Hour or announce its approach, without determining, investigating, or disclosing its exact time.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya deny him any role in fixing its timing; Ibn Atiyya and Bint al-Shati specify warning those who fear it, and Bint al-Shati cites Abu Hayyan that such people benefit from warning. Al-Alusi says his role was to announce its approach; al-Baghawi says he has no knowledge of the Hour. Al-Biqa'i says he was not commissioned to determine its exact time. {"id": "79:44/q06", "question": "What temporal limits or descriptions of the Hour bear on this verse?", "turns_on": "The notes address different aspects of temporal description: the limit supplied by cosmic upheaval and the suddenness of arrival.", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q06/p1", "position": "Its only direct Qur'anic temporal limit is the world's extinction and cosmic upheaval; descriptions of a brief interval are figurative.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 39:68 for the upheaval and 46:35 and 30:55–56 for the brief interval."}, {"id": "79:44/q06/p2", "position": "The Hour arrives suddenly, supporting God's exclusive knowledge of it.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 7:187 but says the argument needs further reflection to reconcile other verses."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q07", "question": "What inward meaning is given to knowledge of the Hour ending with God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q07/p1", "position": "Knowing the Hour requires one's knowledge to be annihilated in divine knowledge and one's self in God.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani draws this from the claim that knowledge of the Hour ends with God."}]}
{"id": "79:44/q08", "question": "How does the verse fit the surah's overall argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:44/q08/p1", "position": "It belongs to the surah's establishment of resurrection and gathering and its display of humanity's final fate.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the preceding surahs fully expounded this theme and this surah's oaths mark its decisive climax."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q01", "question": "How is أن جاءه construed?", "turns_on": "Whether أن is causal or temporal; for the causal construal, its case and which preceding verb governs it; an interrogative reading requires an implied clause.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q01/p1", "position": "It gives the cause: he frowned or turned away because the blind man came.", "reasons": "Al-Farra, al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Tabataba'i give the causal sense. Jishumi glosses the frown and turning of the face on his arrival. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas call it accusative; al-Nahhas supplies an omitted li-anna. Al-Nasafi calls it a purpose expression. Al-Samin says both actions followed the arrival, and notes the familiar case dispute after deletion of the preposition. Al-Qurtubi explicitly calls the causal expression an accusative complement."}, {"id": "80:2/q01/p2", "position": "The causal expression is governed by تولى, the nearer verb.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi names the nearest verb; al-Samin prefers the Basran analysis because it avoids ellipsis for the second competing verb; Bursevi also attributes it to Basran grammarians. Al-Baydawi allows this attachment. Ibn Jinni explicitly prefers the nearer verb and rejects attaching the expression to both verbs together."}, {"id": "80:2/q01/p3", "position": "The causal expression is governed by عبس.", "reasons": "Al-Samin attributes this to Kufan grammarians; al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi record the alternative attachment. Ibn Jinni reports this alternative with the object of تولى left implicit."}, {"id": "80:2/q01/p4", "position": "An omitted lām governs أن in the genitive, relating the arrival to both verbs.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas reports genitive through omitted lām. Ibn Ashur calls lām deletion regular and links both verbs by syntactic competition."}, {"id": "80:2/q01/p5", "position": "أن means إذ, ‘when.’", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas records this as a third analysis; Makki transmits it according to al-Samin."}, {"id": "80:2/q01/p6", "position": "On the interrogative reading an omitted verb is supplied from ‘he frowned and turned away.’", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi supplies the omitted clause and gives the sense ‘Has the blind man just come to him?’ Al-Qurtubi reports al-Hasan's analysis and pause after تولى. Ibn Jinni describes al-Hasan's question as incredulous and supplies the omitted verb from عبس وتولى."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q02", "question": "How is the opening أن read and where is the pause?", "turns_on": "The opening hamza's number and length, interrogative force, and whether recitation pauses after تولى.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q02/p1", "position": "The usual declarative reading has one short hamza and continues without a pause after تولى.", "reasons": "Al-Samin calls this the usual reading; al-Qurtubi says its recitation does not pause after تولى."}, {"id": "80:2/q02/p2", "position": "It is read interrogatively with a lengthened opening hamza and a pause after تولى.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and al-Tabari compare an interrogative reading of 68:14. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi attribute this to al-Hasan, Ibn Atiyya also to Isa. Ibn al-Jawzi lists Ubayy, al-Hasan, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu Imran. Al-Tabrisi calls al-Hasan's reading noncanonical. Reports vary in describing its hamza and length. Ibn Jinni describes al-Hasan's opening as madd, with the stop after وتولى."}, {"id": "80:2/q02/p3", "position": "It is read interrogatively with two open hamzas, sometimes with an intervening alif.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi names Ibn Masud and Ibn al-Sumayfi for two short hamzas. Al-Samin names Zayd ibn Ali, Isa and Abu Imran al-Jawni for two hamzas and cites al-Zamakhshari's آأن with intervening alif; al-Baydawi reports that form. Al-Farra's report also describes two open hamzas. The interrogative asks whether the arrival caused the frown."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q03", "question": "Who is the blind man?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q03/p1", "position": "He is Ibn Umm Maktum, the blind Muslim who came seeking instruction.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Qatada place him in Banu Fihr; reports variously supply personal names and lineages, treated separately below. Ibn Ashur says the definite description refers to a particular known visitor. Islahi reports exegetical agreement. The occasion reports connect his visit to instruction, guidance or recitation."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q04", "question": "What personal name is reported for Ibn Umm Maktum?", "turns_on": "The differing personal names and lineages transmitted for the man called Ibn Umm Maktum.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q04/p1", "position": "He is Abd Allah ibn Shurayh ibn Malik ibn Rabiah, with lineage variants.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi supplies the Fihri lineage; al-Tabataba'i quotes al-Majma with it, and Asad calls him Abd Allah ibn Shurayh. Bursevi and Alusi list Abd Allah ibn Shurayh ibn Malik among alternative names. Names and ancestor spellings vary in reports."}, {"id": "80:2/q04/p2", "position": "He is Amr ibn Qays ibn Zaida.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives Amr ibn Qays; Bursevi identifies this person as Khadija's cousin. Alusi says this is the most famous identification according to Jami al-usul. Muqatil's account also calls him Umm Maktum's son Amr ibn Qays. Al-Qurtubi gives the fuller name Amr ibn Qays ibn Zaida ibn al-Asamm and identifies him as Khadija's maternal cousin."}, {"id": "80:2/q04/p3", "position": "He is Abd Allah ibn Zayd or Zaida.", "reasons": "Qatada's report in al-Tabari has Abd Allah ibn Zayd; al-Mawardi records Abdallah ibn Zaida of Banu Fihr. The forms vary."}, {"id": "80:2/q04/p4", "position": "He is Abd Allah ibn Amr.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this as another name; Alusi lists it among the alternatives."}, {"id": "80:2/q04/p5", "position": "He is Abd Allah ibn Abi Musrah al-Amar.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives this name alongside Amr ibn Qays and lineages."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q05", "question": "Who was Umm Maktum?", "turns_on": "The genealogy behind the man's kunya; reports also differ on the mother's given name.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q05/p1", "position": "She was his mother.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi names her as mother; al-Sadi corrects al-Kashshaf and cites Ibn Abd al-Barr, calling her Atika bint Amir. Alusi calls Umm Maktum the mother's kunya but names Atika bint Abd Allah al-Makhzumiyya. The reported personal name varies. Al-Qurtubi names his mother Atika daughter of Amir of Makhzum."}, {"id": "80:2/q05/p2", "position": "She was his paternal grandmother.", "reasons": "Al-Farra identifies her this way. Bursevi cites al-Sadi's objection to the Kashshaf's version, and Alusi says al-Zamakhshari was wrong on this point."}]}

{"id": "80:2/q07", "question": "Was Ibn Umm Maktum born blind?", "turns_on": "Conflicting biographical reports about when his blindness began.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q07/p1", "position": "He was born blind.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this and says it explains his mother's kunya."}, {"id": "80:2/q07/p2", "position": "He became blind after once seeing.", "reasons": "Alusi records this as the alternative report."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q08", "question": "Why call the visitor ‘the blind man’?", "turns_on": "Whether the description primarily explains his interruption, heightens his claim to compassion, or sharpens the reproach.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q08/p1", "position": "His blindness excuses his interruption and makes his need for care especially clear.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqai and Ibn Ashur say it prompts compassion or softens the rebuke; al-Biqai says it explains his insistence and repairs his hurt. Elmali extends the lesson to all guidance seekers with excuses or needs. Al-Tabataba'i stresses his fear of God and need for guidance."}, {"id": "80:2/q08/p2", "position": "The description sharpens reproach for turning away from someone blind.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi says it may suggest that blindness itself prompted the aversion; al-Tabataba'i says the fearful seeker deserved special attention. Ibn Atiyya contrasts disability with the unbeliever's wealth and human inclination to slight disability."}, {"id": "80:2/q08/p3", "position": "Naming an impairment is permissible when useful or as a clear identifying nickname.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites transmitters known as al-Amash, al-Araj and al-Aftas."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q09", "question": "Who frowned and turned away?", "turns_on": "Whether third-person wording and the Prophet's established character allow or rule out identifying him as the actor; an al-Sadiq report names an Umayyad man.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q09/p1", "position": "The Prophet did so when Ibn Umm Maktum came.", "reasons": "The common occasion reports make the Prophet the subject. Bursevi explicitly identifies the pronoun. Islahi says the later ‘you know’ addresses the Prophet. The third-person opening is explained as a rhetorical choice by several authors."}, {"id": "80:2/q09/p2", "position": "Someone else, specifically an Umayyad man in al-Sadiq's report, frowned and turned away.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq's account places the Umayyad man with the Prophet. Jishumi and al-Tabrisi point to the third-person wording and the Prophet's praised character (68:4; 3:159); al-Murtada says neglecting poor Muslims does not resemble his conduct. Al-Tabataba'i adds early Meccan commands in 26:214–15 and 15:88,94 and argues that wealth preference is rationally ugly even without a prohibition."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q10", "question": "What happened when the blind man came?", "turns_on": "Competing accounts of the occasion and the actor; transmission assessments and variant details of the interruption.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q10/p1", "position": "He sought instruction while the Prophet invited Quraysh leaders; the Prophet turned from him and revelation followed.", "reasons": "Reports say he repeatedly asked for guidance, Qur'an teaching, a recitation or explanation, unaware the Prophet was occupied. The Prophet hoped the leaders' conversion would draw followers. Al-Tirmidhi notes that a version via Hisham ibn Urwa omits Aisha, as does the Muwatta; Ibn Kathir calls the Ibn Abbas report via al-Awfi strange and objectionable because its chain was criticized. Asad calls the traditions well authenticated. Al-Tabataba'i notes Sunni and some Shi'i versions of this account; versions differ on which leaders were present. Urwa's account through Malik and Hisham says Ibn Umm Maktum asked to be brought near. Al-Tirmidhi calls the version from Aisha gharīb, as al-Qurtubi reports."}, {"id": "80:2/q10/p2", "position": "He came after hearing two angels in the Sacred Mosque and sought repentance; the Prophet returned to al-Abbas and Umayya, and the man left despairing.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives the distinctive angelic scene: one angel mentioned Abu Talib's calling people to Islam without seeing them. The man repeated his plea before departing, then the verses came."}, {"id": "80:2/q10/p3", "position": "He came with a seeing guide, pressed past the guide despite a restraining gesture, and the Prophet frowned.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's report says the Prophet gestured to the guide to hold him back; al-Qurtubi calls the man's persistence somewhat rough."}, {"id": "80:2/q10/p4", "position": "The Umayyad man with the Prophet recoiled from Ibn Umm Maktum and frowned; God condemned that conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Sadiq's account is quoted by al-Tabrisi and al-Tabataba'i; it differs over who performed the frown, while keeping Ibn Umm Maktum's entry."}]}
{"id": "80:2/q11", "question": "Which leaders were present in the encounter?", "turns_on": "The different names and numbers supplied by occasion reports. Ibn al-Arabi objects to identifications involving al-Walid, Umayya or al-Abbas on a Medina chronology, whereas Alusi says Ibn Umm Maktum was Meccan and could meet them.", "positions": [{"id": "80:2/q11/p1", "position": "Quraysh leaders or a wealthy notable, without names.", "reasons": "Many accounts leave the leaders unnamed. Al-Dahhak speaks of one wealthy polytheist; Aisha's report through Ibn Kathir adds that the notables saw no fault in what the Prophet said.
